You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
Write a file eval.scm that is a metacircular evaluator capable of interpreting the scheme-like language implemented by interp.py.
The eval.scm file should read exactly one line from STDIN, this will be a file path to a new .scm file that should be interpreted.
Remaining input should be redirected to the interpreted-program, and any output from the program should be sent back to STDOUT.
Your interpreter should be able to interpret (1) each of the test programs in test/, and (2) itself.
For example, the following three commands should all do the same thing:
echo '(+ 7 8)' | python3 interp.py test/calculator.scm
echo -e 'test/calculator.scm\n(+ 7 8)' | python3 interp.py eval.scm
echo -e 'eval.scm\ntest/calculator.scm\n(+ 7 8)' | python3 interp.py eval.scm
The first of these will add 7 and 8 because that is what calculator.scm does.
The second will run eval.scm, which takes test/calculator.scm as the file to run, and runs it; that program then computes 7+8.
The third will run eval.scm, which then takes eval.scm as the input, the outer eval.scm interprets the inner eval.scm which then runs the calculator as above.

  (cond ((= n 0) (cont 0))
        ((= n 1) (cont 1))
        (else
         (fib-cps (- n 1)
                  (lambda (a)
                    (fib-cps (- n 2)
                             (lambda (b)
                               (cont (+ a b)))))))))

(display (fib-cps 6 (lambda (x) x)))

  (if (null? lst)

      (sum-cps (cdr lst)
               (lambda (rest-sum)
                 (cont (+ (car lst) rest-sum))))))

steps.reasoning_content:
We need implement eval.scm. Need think deeply about architecture and constraints.

Task: Write a file eval.scm that is a metacircular evaluator capable of interpreting the scheme-like language implemented by interp.py. eval.scm is itself run by interp.py. It reads exactly one line from STDIN: file path to new .scm file interpreted. Remaining input redirected to interpreted program, output back stdout. Should interpret test programs and itself.

Important: eval.scm runs under interp.py. It can only use primitives implemented by interp.py. We need write Scheme code, not Python. The metacircular evaluator should parse .scm source file manually and evaluate expressions, using host Scheme primitives.

Could potentially call host eval? Not available. Need implement parser & evaluator in Scheme itself.

Need account for Python interp quirks:
- `read` host primitive reads one line from actual stdin, tokenizes line, parses only first expression; if additional expressions after first on same line ignored. But our eval.scm will likely not use host `read` except to read file path; after that use host `fopen/fread` to read file content maybe. However `fread` reads one expression at a time from a file, parses per line and supports multi-line only based on parentheses count. But our parser needs to read arbitrary source and evaluate all expressions. Could use `read` to get path only and then maybe `fopen`/`fread` from file.

But critical: remaining input must be available to interpreted program. If eval.scm reads exactly one line from stdin using host `read`, then later interpreted program's host `read` calls should get remaining stdin. Host interp.py reads the entire file eval.scm through `run_file` before execution; standard input untouched until eval.scm executes. When `(read)` executes, Python input() reads a line from sys.stdin. Good. So `(define file (read))` will return string? Actually host parser tokenizer: bare filename like `test/calculator.scm` is parsed as symbol string (not String), which is okay; quotes maybe path string literal returns String object. Need convert to str? fopen handles both.

Then our evaluator can read source file. Options:
1. `(fopen file "r")` -> file id, then repeatedly `(fread id)` returns one expression parsed by host. Host's fread handles comments, strings, quotes, parentheses across lines. But host fread has flawed parenthesis count for quotes? Quote token doesn't affect parens; okay. Dotted pairs not supported by parse_expr at all! Important: interp.py tokenizer treats "." as part of symbol because not in "()';"; parse_expr does not implement dot syntax. Yet test/10 has `'((name . "John") ...)`. Running test/10 directly with interp.py likely fails? Let's see. Actually parse_expr tokenizes tokens: "(", "(", "name", ".", String("John"), ")", ...; "." parsed as symbol ".", so expression `(name . "John")` becomes 3-element list `(name . "John")` stored as Pair("name", Pair(".", Pair(String("John"), None))). It does not represent dotted pair. Then `assoc-get` expects `(cdr (car alist))`, for first entry cdr is Pair(".", Pair(String,None)), not String. display may show list `(. "John")` maybe but perhaps no output of name? Let's run later. But we need replicate interpreter semantics exactly, perhaps test advanced may not be run due no dotted pairs. However we need interpret all test programs and itself. Could not support dot if host doesn't.

But fread's implementation may be problematic across multiple expressions on same line: it calls `tokenize(line.strip())`, accumulates tokens and only returns an expression when paren_count == 0. Suppose line `(define x 1) (define y 2)`: tokens two expressions, paren count after first reaches 0 then second reaches 0 too; after line it parses first expression and returns, dropping second tokens next fread continues next line, lost second. But grep found `) *(` only in nested contexts on same line, i.e., lambda application etc not separate top-level expressions. Most files have one top-level expression per line. Some multi-line expressions. Good.

Could simply use host fread repeatedly to parse one expression and then our own eval. That avoids writing our own parser entirely. But requirement "metacircular evaluator capable of interpreting ... and itself". A metacircular evaluator generally includes eval/apply. If using host's parser/fread but own eval/apply, still okay maybe. Need interpret itself: eval.scm as source file read by eval.scm. Host fread should parse eval.scm okay.

However potential issue: host fread loses tokens after a complete line if line has multiple expressions; our eval.scm may have top-level expressions on same line? We'll write one per line. But comments and string literals? fread tokenizes okay. Multi-line top-level expression? host fread handles via balances.

Alternative write own parser using `read`/`getchr`, but harder. Host fread gives parser for free. Need ensure `fread` can parse all source. Strings tokenizer handles escapes strangely but okay. It can't parse dotted pairs, but host direct also can't represent them properly.

Need evaluate forms exactly matching interp.py semantics. Could build evaluator in Scheme:
- `eval` function takes expression `x`, environment `env`.
- Need distinguish int, bool, string? (host has symbol?, string?, number?, pair?, null?). Note booleans are Python bool and number? lambda checks `isinstance(x,int)`, bool is subclass of int in Python! Actually isinstance(True, int) -> True. So number? #t returns true. But not vital.
- host `eq?` uses Python equality: strings/symbols equal based on string. Pair equality object identity (no __eq__) unless cyclic. `equal?` same. Tests use eq? on symbols, strings maybe.
- Store environment as association list of pairs. Could use host pairs. `lookup`, `extend`, `define`, `set`.
- Need variable binding with symbols represented as host strings (because host parser returns Python str for symbols). So symbols are strings. Environment keys strings. But data expressions as strings can represent atoms; in AST, symbols are str too; quote returns underlying data type. Strings are custom String objects. Need `self-evaluating?` for number and String. `number?` primitive sees bool as number; but booleans need self-evaluate too. We can check `(or (number? x) (string? x))`; but boolean #t is number? true so it would be self-evaluating and returned. #f maybe number? true too? isinstance(False, int) yes, so both self-evaluating. But number? on a Python bool true. So okay. But what about `#t` as symbol? parser returns bool. Fine.
- For symbols: `(symbol? x)`.
- For pairs: `(pair? x)`, special forms via `(car x)`.
- Applications evaluate operator and args in env, apply procedure.
- Closure representation: Need represent host Procedure? We cannot construct host Procedure from Scheme code directly except via lambda syntax, which creates host procedure for eval.scm's own functions, but our meta-evaluator can represent user closures using an internal data structure, e.g., a list tagged 'closure: `(list 'closure params body env)`. Then `apply` dispatches if host procedure? We can check `procedure?`? Not provided. Could call host procedures directly if expression function value is host Procedure from eval.scm or host primitive. Need identify closures. We could represent all user closures as Scheme lambda values? But we need environment mutable for lexical scoping and apply at runtime. Host lambda closures are fixed to eval.scm source environment, not user environment. Can't create arbitrary host Procedure manually aside from call to `(eval (list 'lambda ...))` which doesn't work. Could use host callable? No.
- So internal closures tagged lists. Need distinguish from normal lists. Use a unique tag. Could tag as pair `(cons 'closure (cons params (cons body env)))`, and function `closure?`.
- Host primitives are callable procedures (Python functions) represented directly in environment and can be applied via `apply` using generic? In Scheme, to call a host procedure with dynamic args (args list), we need `apply` primitive, not provided! Ah no `apply` in interp.py global env. We can't dynamically apply a host procedure to a list of arguments unless we write explicit dispatch based on primitive names. Alternative store primitive names and dispatch manually for each builtin. But that's an evaluator: when operator is a symbol naming primitive, can handle direct. Higher-order functions: user passes primitives as values to user-defined functions (`(define (fold-left f init lst) ... (f init (car lst)) ...)`), then evaluator applies f which may be primitive or closure. Since no apply primitive, we must implement our own `meta-apply` that can call host primitive functions dynamically. Could construct a host Scheme expression `(f arg1 arg2 ...)` and somehow invoke? Host has no eval.
- But we can implement `apply` by direct dispatch in Scheme code for each primitive. If procedure value is a Python callable or host closure from eval.scm, we can't inspect arity or call dynamically. However most callables in our environment are host primitives and our own helper procedures. If our evaluator needs to call host primitives with dynamic args, explicit case dispatch based on a representation works: store primitives as tagged lists or just symbols and dispatch by symbol name. Then when a user passes `+`, evaluator quotes/returns atom symbol? In our evaluator, evaluating symbol `+` returns environment binding. We could bind primitives to symbolic tags e.g. `(list 'primitive '+)`. Then `meta-apply` checks tag and dispatches. For host procedures defined in eval.scm (helper functions), our evaluator does not need to call them as user values; they are only in eval.scm implementation, not in user program env. But our evaluator code itself calls them directly in source (host compile-time closures), not through user env. So no need meta-apply host lambdas. Unless user accesses a primitive that is a host lambda from interp.py global env (e.g. `=` etc). We can rebind them to symbolic tags in our initial environment, not rely on host env. Thus meta evaluator can use own primitive dispatch.
- But we need primitives for arithmetic/list operations, file I/O, etc. Could implement all needed primitives ourselves using host primitives. However some host primitives like `fopen`, `fread`, `display`, `newline`, `read`, `getchr`, `putchr`, `symbol`, `set-car!`, `set-cdr!`, etc. can be directly called from eval.scm implementation code because eval.scm is itself interpreted by host and lexical top-level env contains them. Our evaluator's primitive dispatch can directly call these host functions, and because host lacks `apply`, we can only call them with explicit arguments. That's fine for fixed-arity primitives. For variadic primitives like `+`, `*`, we need dynamic arity; host `+` is a Python lambda accepting *args, but no apply. Our evaluator can implement primitive dispatch with case for each symbol:
  - `+`: We need sum args list. We can write a recursive helper `(sum-list args)` using host `+` with exactly 2 args, but host + is variadic; in eval.scm source we call `(+ a b)` fine.
  - `-`, etc.
  - `display`: host display function exactly 1 arg; call directly.
  - `newline`: 0.
  - user program calls `(display ...)`, our meta evaluator dispatch sees primitive tag `display`, calls `(display arg)` directly (host).
  - `read` no args: call host `(read)`.
  - `fopen` call host directly.
  - `symbol` etc.
  - `set-car!` etc.
- But host Scheme source in eval.scm cannot call arbitrary Python callable with dynamic args. So primitive dispatch must be explicit per primitive.

This seems doable. But major subtlety: our evaluator's environment representation uses host pairs and symbols. Host pair mutation may be used by user programs through set-car!/set-cdr!. We can represent user env as list of bindings and mutate to implement define/set!. But `set-car!` on arbitrary data also needs work. Host pairs support mutation.

Need parse source file. Could rely on host `fread` to read expressions. But then our evaluator is not fully reading source content itself; phrase "capable of interpreting the scheme-like language implemented by interp.py" can be satisfied. Yet evaluator should be capable of interpreting itself. If eval.scm source contains primitives/forms and our own eval dispatch, host fread parsing is enough. But note: `fread` only returns expression when parentheses balanced; if a file expression doesn't involve parentheses, such as bare atom? Test files top-level are all parenthesized. eval.scm ours should have all top-level parenthesized. Strings on multiple lines? unlikely.

Could instead use `(read)` on file content, but easier fread.

Then `(define f (fopen file "r"))`; but fopen mode expects String or plain str. In eval.scm source, `"r"` parsed by host tokenizer as String object. Good. If file path `test/calculator.scm` returned as Python str; fopen detects if String only, leaves str. Good.

Then repeatedly `(fread f)` until `#f`? Host fread returns None at EOF, which is represented as None/Pair null. In Scheme, `null? #f`? `fread` returns None -> `null?` true. So loop.

```
; eval.scm - metacircular evaluator for interp.py

(define (lookup-binding name bindings)
  (if (null? bindings)
      '()
      (if (eq? name (car (car bindings)))
          (car bindings)
          (lookup-binding name (cdr bindings)))))

(define (env-lookup name env)
  (let ((b (lookup-binding name (car env))))
    (if (null? b)
        (if (null? (cdr env))
            '()
            (env-lookup name (cdr env)))
        (cdr b))))

(define (env-define env name val)
  (set-car! env (cons (cons name val) (car env))))

(define (env-set name val env)
  (let ((b (lookup-binding name (car env))))
    (if (null? b)
        (if (null? (cdr env))
            '()
            (env-set name val (cdr env)))
        (set-cdr! b val))))

(define (bind-params params args env)
  (if (null? params)
      '()
      (progn
        (env-define env (car params) (car args))
        (bind-params (cdr params) (cdr args) env))))

(define (make-closure params body env)
  (cons 'closure (cons params (cons body env))))

(define (closure? x)
  (if (pair? x)
      (eq? (car x) 'closure)
      #f))

(define (closure-params p) (car (cdr p)))
(define (closure-body p) (car (cdr (cdr p))))
(define (closure-env p) (car (cdr (cdr (cdr p)))))

(define (eval-sequence body env)
  (if (null? body)
      '()
      (let ((result (m-eval (car body) env)))
        (if (null? (cdr body))
            result
            (eval-sequence (cdr body) env)))))

(define (eval-args arglist env)
  (if (null? arglist)
      '()
      (cons (m-eval (car arglist) env)
            (eval-args (cdr arglist) env))))

(define (m-eval expr env)
  (cond ((eq? expr #t) #t)
        ((eq? expr #f) #f)
        ((number? expr) expr)
        ((string? expr) expr)
        ((symbol? expr) (env-lookup expr env))
        ((pair? expr) (m-eval-pair expr env))
        (else expr)))

(define (m-eval-pair expr env)
  (let ((op (car expr)))
    (cond ((eq? op 'quote) (car (cdr expr)))
          ((eq? op 'if) (m-eval-if expr env))
          ((eq? op 'define) (m-eval-define expr env))
          ((eq? op 'set!) (m-eval-set expr env))
          ((eq? op 'lambda) (make-closure (car (cdr expr)) (cdr (cdr expr)) env))
          ((eq? op 'let) (m-eval-let expr env))
          ((eq? op 'begin) (eval-sequence (cdr expr) env))
          ((eq? op 'progn) (eval-sequence (cdr expr) env))
          ((eq? op 'cond) (m-eval-cond (cdr expr) env))
          (else (m-apply (m-eval op env)
                         (eval-args (cdr expr) env))))))
```
